title: Apply knowledge of statistics and probability to critically interrogate and effectively communicate findings on life related problems

lessons.title: Asking questions and collecting good data
lessons.html:
Statistics starts with a good question

Farm managers and supervisors use data all the time: milk yield per cow, mass gain of weaners, germination of seed lots, carcass grades, rainfall, and number of injuries per month. Statistics helps you turn these numbers into decisions. The first step is a clear question, for example: ‘Do heifers on the new supplement gain more mass than those on the old one?’ or ‘Is the germination of our sunflower lots falling over the years?’

Population and sample

The population is the whole group you want to know about, such as all 600 ewes on the farm. A sample is the part you actually measure, such as 60 ewes. A sample is useful only if it represents the population.

Sampling methods

  • Simple random: every member has an equal chance, for example drawing ear-tag numbers from a hat or using a random number generator.
  • Systematic: every tenth animal through the crush, or every fifth bag on a pallet.
  • Stratified: divide into groups (for example camps or age groups) and sample from each group.

Bias

Bias is a systematic error that pushes results one way. Examples on a farm:

  • weighing only the calves that come to the gate first, which are often the strongest;
  • counting pests only on the edge of an orchard block, where infestation is usually higher;
  • asking workers about safety in front of the manager, so they give the expected answer;
  • a sample that is too small, so chance has a big effect.

Types of data

TypeExample
CategoricalBreed, carcass grade, cultivar
Discrete numericalNumber of lambs born, number of injuries
Continuous numericalMass in kg, milk in litres, temperature

Recording data

Design a simple record sheet before you start, with columns for date, identity (tag or lot number), measurement and unit, and the name of the recorder. Use calibrated scales and thermometers, and record the reading exactly. Poor data cannot be fixed by clever calculations later.

lessons.title: Summarising and displaying data
lessons.html:
Making sense of a list of numbers

Suppose the daily milk yields in litres for seven cows are: 18, 22, 20, 25, 19, 22, 30.

Measures of centre

  • Mean (average): add all values and divide by how many. 156 ÷ 7 = about 22.3 litres.
  • Median: the middle value when sorted. Sorted: 18, 19, 20, 22, 22, 25, 30. The median is 22 litres.
  • Mode: the value that occurs most often: 22 litres.

The mean is pulled up or down by extreme values (outliers). One cow producing 30 litres raises the mean above the median. When data has outliers, such as farm incomes in a district, the median often gives a fairer picture.

Measures of spread

  • Range = largest − smallest = 30 − 18 = 12 litres.
  • Quartiles: the lower quartile (Q1) is the middle of the lower half (19) and the upper quartile (Q3) the middle of the upper half (25). The interquartile range (IQR) = Q3 − Q1 = 6 litres. It shows the spread of the middle half of the data.
  • Standard deviation measures how far values typically lie from the mean; a calculator or spreadsheet works it out. A small standard deviation means a uniform herd or lot.

Choosing a graph

GraphUse it for
Bar graphComparing categories, such as yield per cultivar
Pie chartParts of a whole, such as share of costs
HistogramDistribution of continuous data, such as weaner masses
Line graphChange over time, such as monthly rainfall
Scatter plotRelationship between two variables, such as rainfall and yield
Box-and-whisker plotComparing spread and median of groups

Every graph needs a title, labelled axes with units, a sensible scale that usually starts at zero for bar graphs, and the source of the data.

Correlation is not causation

A scatter plot may show that farms with more tractors have higher yields. That does not prove tractors cause high yields; larger, better-financed farms may simply have both. Look for other explanations before concluding that one thing causes another.

lessons.title: Probability and communicating findings critically
lessons.html:
Working with chance

Probability measures how likely an event is, on a scale from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). It can be written as a fraction, decimal or percentage.

Basic rules

  • Probability of an event = number of favourable outcomes ÷ total number of equally likely outcomes. The chance of a heifer calf from one birth is about 1 in 2, or 0.5.
  • Probability an event does not happen = 1 − probability it happens. If a seed lot germinates at 92%, the probability a seed fails is 0.08.
  • For two independent events, multiply: the probability that two seeds both germinate is 0.92 × 0.92 = about 0.85.
  • Expected value: if you plant 100 000 seeds at 92% germination, you expect about 92 000 seedlings, before field losses.

Risk in real life

Farmers make decisions under uncertainty: Will it rain enough? Will the price hold? Will a disease outbreak close export markets? Long-term records can give relative frequencies, for example ‘in 7 of the last 30 years, rainfall in this district was below 400 mm’, giving an estimated probability of about 0.23 for a dry year. Insurance, crop choice and stocking rates are all based on such estimates.

Interrogating statistics critically

When you read a claim in a sales brochure, news report or management presentation, ask:

  1. How big was the sample, and how was it chosen?
  2. Which average was used, and why?
  3. Is the graph's scale honest?
  4. Are percentages based on small numbers? ‘Injuries up 100%’ might mean from 1 to 2.
  5. Who paid for the study, and do they benefit?
  6. Does the claim confuse correlation with causation?

Communicating your findings

Report findings clearly to the audience that must act on them. State the question, how data was collected, the main results with one or two well-chosen graphs, the limitations (such as a small sample or one season only), and your conclusion and recommendation. Example: ‘Over 12 weeks, 40 weaners on supplement B gained a median of 0.9 kg/day compared with 0.8 kg/day on supplement A. Because the trial was one season on one farm, we recommend repeating it before changing all feeding.’

Key points

  • Start with a clear question and a representative, unbiased sample.
  • Use mean, median and mode for centre; range, IQR and standard deviation for spread.
  • Choose a graph that fits the data and label it fully.
  • Probability runs from 0 to 1; P(not A) = 1 − P(A); multiply for independent events.
  • Question sample size, scales, small-number percentages and correlation claims.
